A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Label-Trim research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across the layout changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original outlier-detection experiments on three tabular datasets and six visual-data pairings in Section 4 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds evaluations with additional scoring models, harder contamination scenarios, and test-time outlier shifts.

M1.justification: Section 3.3, Equation (4), and Algorithms 1–2 retain the same procedure: annotate the highest-scoring calibration points, remove confirmed outliers, and calibrate using the retained set. Additional scoring models test the existing model-agnostic procedure.

E1.justification: The three tabular datasets and six visual-data pairings remain. However, v2 adds distinct scenarios with score-selected contaminants resembling inliers across the tabular datasets and changing test-time outlier populations on shuttle (Figures 16–20), substantially extending coverage beyond random contamination.

E2.justification: The comparison methods remain Standard, Oracle, Naive-Trim, and Small-Clean. LOF, One-Class SVM, ReAct/VGG-19, and SCALE/ResNet-18 are additional scoring configurations shared by Label-Trim and its comparators.

E3.justification: v2 adds evaluations using LOF and One-Class SVM on tabular data and ReAct/VGG-19 and SCALE/ResNet-18 on visual data. New protocols include contamination rates up to 15%, percentile-based outlier selection, and shuttle tests varying outlier percentile ranges while training/calibration outliers come from the 30th–100th percentiles. These supplement the retained original protocols.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained contamination, labeling-budget, significance-level, and KDDCup99 variability analyses, v2 tests sensitivity to scoring models, heavier contamination, harder contaminants, and test-time outlier shifts. Figures 13–20 substantially expand robustness evidence and reveal settings with weak detection power.

E5.justification: Both versions generally use 100 random data splits, retain 400-split KDDCup99 labeling-budget analyses, and report standard errors in visual-data tables. The added results follow the existing reporting practices; no new statistical estimation procedure or increased repeat count is documented.

E6.justification: Original numerical tables are retained, including v1 Tables 4–9 as v2 Tables 6–11. Substantial new results appear in Figures 13–20 and Tables 4–5 and 12–23. For example, at alpha = 0.01 and 5% contamination, the new ReAct/VGG-19 and SCALE/ResNet-18 evaluations report Label-Trim relative powers of 1.606 and 1.627, respectively, both with type-I error 0.009.

T1.justification: Proposition 2.1, Lemma 2.2, Assumption 2.3, Theorem 3.1, and Appendix A’s auxiliary propositions, mixture-distribution corollary, and proofs are substantively unchanged. The labeling-budget condition m <= alpha(n + 1) is retained.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution outline, and central discussion retain the same claims: contamination can make conformal calibration conservative, and selective annotation can improve power with approximate type-I error control under stated conditions. The expanded experiments support these existing contributions.

C2.justification: Section 5 newly emphasizes the requirement that calibration and test inliers share an i.i.d. distribution. It also discusses label ambiguity, possible extensions using uncertainty information, and retaining uncertain points as inliers. These additions refine applicability and interpretation.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds implementation information for the new configurations, including the VGG-19 model source, SCALE’s activation-rescaling rule and 65% percentile setting, and the One-Class SVM RBF kernel. Existing split recipes, ReAct’s 90% threshold, and the method’s repository link remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting LOF, One-Class SVM, SCALE, and the VGG-19 implementation. Section 5 also connects the work to ambiguous-ground-truth research by Stutz, Javanmardi, and Caprio and colleagues. The main related-work positioning in Section 1.3 remains stable.

P1.justification: Most original exposition is retained, with grammatical corrections, added pointers to experiments, and expanded discussion. The former tabular and visual appendices become subsections B.2.1 and B.2.2 under Additional Experiments. These are limited narrative and organizational changes.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main text and repositions figures, tables, and algorithms. It adds the method schematic in Figure 2, robustness Figures 13–20, and fourteen new tables. Existing graphics are retained and renumbered, while table captions more explicitly identify scoring configurations.

improvement.justification: v1’s empirical support relied on one scoring configuration per data modality and random contamination. v2 substantially strengthens that support by testing alternative scorers, harder contaminants, heavier contamination, and shifted test outliers, exposing low-power regimes alongside successes. These tests address important questions about robustness while preserving the original evidence. The schematic and clearer limitations further improve the paper, although the theoretical guarantees remain unchanged and require matching inlier distributions.
